claim: Several previous studies reported a time-dependent loss of CA signals on cytoplasmic structures positive for the HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr in HeLa- or HOS-derived cell lines infected with VSV-G pseudotyped VLPs.
source: Several previous studies reported a time-dependent loss of CA signals on cytoplasmic structures positive for the HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr in HeLa- or HOS-derived cell lines infected with VSV-G pseudotyped VLPs (McDonald et al., 2002; Hulme et al., 2011), suggesting gradual capsid uncoating during reverse transcription.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies suggested gradual capsid uncoating during reverse transcription.
source: Several previous studies reported a time-dependent loss of CA signals on cytoplasmic structures positive for the HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr in HeLa- or HOS-derived cell lines infected with VSV-G pseudotyped VLPs (McDonald et al., 2002; Hulme et al., 2011), suggesting gradual capsid uncoating during reverse transcription.
evidence: This is an interpretation from cited previous studies.

claim: The reported loss of CA signal in previous studies may have been due to the inaccessibility of the reactive epitope due to conformational changes and/or host protein binding after cytoplasmic entry.
source: Alternatively, the reported loss of CA signal may have been due to the inaccessibility of the reactive epitope due to conformational changes and/or host protein binding after cytoplasmic entry, especially since monoclonal antibodies were used in these studies.
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative explanations for previous observations.

claim: An influence of the entry pathway may be considered as prior studies used VSV-G pseudotyped particles entering via the endosomal route.
source: An influence of the entry pathway may also be considered as these prior studies used VSV-G pseudotyped particles entering via the endosomal route.
evidence: This is a speculation about factors that may explain differences between studies.

claim: RTC/PIC co-localizing with nuclear pore proteins in TZM-bl cells exhibited a strong CA signal.
source: RTC/PIC co-localizing with nuclear pore proteins in TZM-bl cells also exhibited a strong CA signal, while CA was absent from all but one nuclear PIC indicating that CA is lost at the nuclear pore or shortly after nuclear entry in this cell type.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CA was absent from all but one nuclear PIC in TZM-bl cells.
source: RTC/PIC co-localizing with nuclear pore proteins in TZM-bl cells also exhibited a strong CA signal, while CA was absent from all but one nuclear PIC indicating that CA is lost at the nuclear pore or shortly after nuclear entry in this cell type.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CA is lost at the nuclear pore or shortly after nuclear entry in TZM-bl cells.
source: RTC/PIC co-localizing with nuclear pore proteins in TZM-bl cells also exhibited a strong CA signal, while CA was absent from all but one nuclear PIC indicating that CA is lost at the nuclear pore or shortly after nuclear entry in this cell type.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observation.

claim: The hypothesis that CA is lost at the nuclear pore is consistent with the described interaction of CA with nucleoporins 153 and 358.
source: This hypothesis is consistent with the described interaction of CA with nucleoporins 153 and 358 (Schaller et al., 2011; Matreyek et al., 2013) and suggests that cDNA within the intact viral capsid or a capsid-derived structure docks to the nuclear pore complex followed by dissociation of CA and nuclear import.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: cDNA within the intact viral capsid or a capsid-derived structure docks to the nuclear pore complex followed by dissociation of CA and nuclear import.
source: This hypothesis is consistent with the described interaction of CA with nucleoporins 153 and 358 (Schaller et al., 2011; Matreyek et al., 2013) and suggests that cDNA within the intact viral capsid or a capsid-derived structure docks to the nuclear pore complex followed by dissociation of CA and nuclear import.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations and cited literature.

claim: Less than half of the RTC/PIC showed a detectable CA signal in primary human MDM.
source: A very different picture was observed for CA association of RTC/PIC in primary human MDM. Less than half of the RTC/PIC showed a detectable CA signal in this case, while >97% of all RTC/PIC were CA-positive in HeLa-derived cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Almost all nuclear PIC (97%) were CA-positive in primary human MDM.
source: This difference is unlikely to be caused by earlier CA uncoating of productive RTC/PIC in MDM, since almost all nuclear PIC (97%) were CA-positive in this cell type.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: A CA-positive nuclear PIC and a CA-negative cytoplasmic RTC/PIC were observed in the same cell.
source: We even observed a CA-positive nuclear PIC and a CA-negative cytoplasmic RTC/PIC in the same cell (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The intact or remodeled viral capsid is imported through the intact nuclear pore in post-mitotic MDM following complete or partial reverse transcription.
source: These observations suggest that the intact or remodeled viral capsid is imported through the intact nuclear pore in post-mitotic MDM following complete or partial reverse transcription.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations in MDM.

claim: The observation that nuclear PIC in MDM were clearly CA-positive while the majority of cytoplasmic RTC/PIC were CA-negative suggests that many of the cytoplasmic RTC/PIC detected in MDM were not predecessors of nuclear PIC but may rather represent dead-end products.
source: The fact that nuclear PIC in MDM were clearly CA-positive, while the majority of cytoplasmic RTC/PIC were CA-negative in the same cells, and CA appeared to be lost over time suggests that many of the cytoplasmic RTC/PIC detected in MDM were not predecessors of nuclear PIC but may rather represent dead-end products.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: CA-negative cytoplasmic RTC/PIC contain incomplete or complete HIV-1 cDNA, which can be exposed to cytoplasmic DNA sensors.
source: These (at least partially) uncoated cytoplasmic structures contain incomplete or complete HIV-1 cDNA, which can be exposed to cytoplasmic DNA sensors.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of CA-negative cytoplasmic RTC/PIC.

claim: CA-negative cytoplasmic RTC/PIC may contribute to the strong innate immune response in MDM.
source: They may thus contribute to the strong innate immune response in MDM (Lahaye et al., 2013; Rasaiyaah et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations.

claim: It is difficult to envision how the CA-negative cytoplasmic RTC/PIC could give rise to nuclear PIC, since almost all nuclear PIC were strongly CA-positive.
source: It is difficult to envision, however, how the CA-negative cytoplasmic RTC/PIC could give rise to nuclear PIC, since almost all nuclear PIC were strongly CA-positive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The capsid or a capsid-derived structure remains intact not only during reverse transcription but also during nuclear import, at least in MDM.
source: Our results therefore suggest that the capsid or a capsid-derived structure remains intact not only during reverse transcription but also during nuclear import, at least in MDM.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations in MDM.

claim: Lack of a CA signal on nuclear PIC in the proliferating HeLa-derived reporter cell line may indicate the loss of the capsid at the nuclear pore, but prior to nuclear import.
source: Lack of a CA signal on nuclear PIC in the proliferating HeLa-derived reporter cell line may indicate the loss of the capsid at the nuclear pore, but prior to nuclear import, or may be due to more rapid removal of CA after nuclear import in these cells compared to MDM.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism in HeLa-derived cells.

claim: Lack of a CA signal on nuclear PIC in the proliferating HeLa-derived reporter cell line may be due to more rapid removal of CA after nuclear import in these cells compared to MDM.
source: Lack of a CA signal on nuclear PIC in the proliferating HeLa-derived reporter cell line may indicate the loss of the capsid at the nuclear pore, but prior to nuclear import, or may be due to more rapid removal of CA after nuclear import in these cells compared to MDM.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism in HeLa-derived cells.

claim: It appears likely that the capsid has to be removed before proviral integration in all productively infected cells.
source: It appears likely that the capsid has to be removed before proviral integration in all productively infected cells, and the two CA-negative nuclear PIC in MDM in the present study may thus reflect a later stage after nuclear entry.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: The two CA-negative nuclear PIC in MDM may reflect a later stage after nuclear entry.
source: It appears likely that the capsid has to be removed before proviral integration in all productively infected cells, and the two CA-negative nuclear PIC in MDM in the present study may thus reflect a later stage after nuclear entry.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: CA-negative nuclear PIC were only detected 48 hr after infection in MDM.
source: Accordingly, CA-negative nuclear PIC were only detected 48 hr after infection, while all nuclear PIC were CA-positive at 24 hr after infection.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: All nuclear PIC were CA-positive at 24 hr after infection in MDM.
source: Accordingly, CA-negative nuclear PIC were only detected 48 hr after infection, while all nuclear PIC were CA-positive at 24 hr after infection.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: PF74 completely blocks HIV-1 infection at a concentration of 10 µM.
source: We confirmed that PF74 completely blocks HIV-1 infection at a concentration of 10 µM (Figure 5A) as previously shown (Shi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and citation.

claim: Inhibition by PF74 affected a stage preceding cDNA synthesis.
source: Inhibition affected a stage preceding cDNA synthesis: detection of RTC/PIC was dramatically reduced in cells infected for 4.5 hr in the presence of 10 µM PF74 (Figure 5B), and this result was confirmed by quantitative determination of HIV-1 specific cDNA using PCR (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Detection of RTC/PIC was dramatically reduced in cells infected for 4.5 hr in the presence of 10 µM PF74.
source: Inhibition affected a stage preceding cDNA synthesis: detection of RTC/PIC was dramatically reduced in cells infected for 4.5 hr in the presence of 10 µM PF74 (Figure 5B), and this result was confirmed by quantitative determination of HIV-1 specific cDNA using PCR (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The remaining RTC/PIC observed at 10 µM PF74 were significantly less frequently positive for CA (65% vs 97% in the control sample).
source: The observation that the remaining RTC/PIC observed at this PF74 concentration were significantly less frequently positive for CA (65% vs 97% in the control sample; p < 0.01) is consistent with the proposed effect of PF74 on capsid uncoating.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The reduced CA positivity of RTC/PIC at 10 µM PF74 is consistent with the proposed effect of PF74 on capsid uncoating.
source: The observation that the remaining RTC/PIC observed at this PF74 concentration were significantly less frequently positive for CA (65% vs 97% in the control sample; p < 0.01) is consistent with the proposed effect of PF74 on capsid uncoating.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observation.

claim: 2 µM PF74 reduced HIV-1 infectivity >95% at the high multiplicity of infection used.
source: 2 µM PF74 reduced HIV-1 infectivity >95% in our experimental system, even at the high multiplicity of infection used.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: RTC/PIC formation was completely unaffected at 2 µM PF74 concentration, despite almost complete loss of infectivity.
source: Unexpectedly, however, RTC/PIC formation was completely unaffected at this PF74 concentration, despite almost complete loss of infectivity.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: EdU-positive RTC/PIC were readily detected in cells infected with HIV-1 for 4.5 hr in the presence of 2 µM PF74 with no apparent difference compared to control infections (7.7 vs 6.8 RTC/PIC per cell on average).
source: EdU-positive RTC/PIC were readily detected in cells infected with HIV-1 for 4.5 hr in the presence of 2 µM PF74 with no apparent difference compared to control infections (7.7 vs 6.8 RTC/PIC per cell on average, respectively; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Infection in the presence of 2 µM PF74 did not affect association of RTC/PIC with CA: 98% and 97% of RTC/PIC exhibited a positive CA signal when cells were infected in the presence or absence of 2 µM PF74, respectively.
source: Furthermore, infection in the presence of 2 µM PF74 did not affect association of RTC/PIC with CA: 98% and 97% of RTC/PIC exhibited a positive CA signal when cells were infected in the presence or absence of 2 µM PF74, respectively (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Reverse transcription was unaffected by ∼2 µM PF74 as confirmed by quantitative PCR analysis.
source: The result that reverse transcription was unaffected by ∼2 µM PF74 was confirmed by quantitative PCR analysis.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No significant difference was observed for late reverse transcription products when cells were infected with HIV-1 in the presence or absence of 2.7 µM PF74.
source: No significant difference was observed for late reverse transcription products when cells were infected with HIV-1 in the presence or absence of 2.7 µM PF74, while these products were lost upon infection in the presence of EFV or at a higher PF74 concentration, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Late reverse transcription products were lost upon infection in the presence of EFV.
source: No significant difference was observed for late reverse transcription products when cells were infected with HIV-1 in the presence or absence of 2.7 µM PF74, while these products were lost upon infection in the presence of EFV or at a higher PF74 concentration, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Late reverse transcription products were lost upon infection in the presence of a higher PF74 concentration.
source: No significant difference was observed for late reverse transcription products when cells were infected with HIV-1 in the presence or absence of 2.7 µM PF74, while these products were lost upon infection in the presence of EFV or at a higher PF74 concentration, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Infection in the presence of 2.7 µM PF74 almost completely abolished the formation of 2-LTR circles despite normal synthesis of late reverse transcription products.
source: Infection in the presence of 2.7 µM PF74 almost completely abolished the formation of 2-LTR circles despite normal synthesis of late reverse transcription products, indicating a specific defect in nuclear import of viral cDNA.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 2.7 µM PF74 causes a specific defect in nuclear import of viral cDNA.
source: Infection in the presence of 2.7 µM PF74 almost completely abolished the formation of 2-LTR circles despite normal synthesis of late reverse transcription products, indicating a specific defect in nuclear import of viral cDNA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observation.

claim: EFV abolished 2-LTR circles.
source: As expected, EFV or 8.1 µM PF74 abolished 2-LTR circles as well, while incubation in the presence of the IN inhibitor elvitegravir (EVG), which blocks chromosomal integration of the HIV-1 cDNA without affecting reverse transcription or nuclear import (Shimura et al., 2008), yielded a strong increase of 2-LTR circles (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 8.1 µM PF74 abolished 2-LTR circles.
source: As expected, EFV or 8.1 µM PF74 abolished 2-LTR circles as well, while incubation in the presence of the IN inhibitor elvitegravir (EVG), which blocks chromosomal integration of the HIV-1 cDNA without affecting reverse transcription or nuclear import (Shimura et al., 2008), yielded a strong increase of 2-LTR circles (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Elvitegravir (EVG) blocks chromosomal integration of the HIV-1 cDNA without affecting reverse transcription or nuclear import.
source: As expected, EFV or 8.1 µM PF74 abolished 2-LTR circles as well, while incubation in the presence of the IN inhibitor elvitegravir (EVG), which blocks chromosomal integration of the HIV-1 cDNA without affecting reverse transcription or nuclear import (Shimura et al., 2008), yielded a strong increase of 2-LTR circles (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Incubation in the presence of elvitegravir (EVG) yielded a strong increase of 2-LTR circles.
source: As expected, EFV or 8.1 µM PF74 abolished 2-LTR circles as well, while incubation in the presence of the IN inhibitor elvitegravir (EVG), which blocks chromosomal integration of the HIV-1 cDNA without affecting reverse transcription or nuclear import (Shimura et al., 2008), yielded a strong increase of 2-LTR circles (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PF74 has a dose-dependent bimodal effect on early HIV-1 infection, targeting reverse transcription and PIC nuclear import, respectively.
source: Taken together these results indicate a dose-dependent bimodal effect of PF74 on early HIV-1 infection, targeting reverse transcription and PIC nuclear import, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The nuclear import defect at low concentrations of PF74 may be caused by binding of this compound to a reactive groove on the viral capsid, leading to competitive inhibition of capsid interaction with the host proteins Nup153 and CPSF6.
source: The nuclear import defect at low concentrations of PF74 may be caused by binding of this compound to a reactive groove on the viral capsid, leading to competitive inhibition of capsid interaction with the host proteins Nup153 and CPSF6 (Matreyek et al., 2013; Price et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Both Nup153 and CPSF6 have been implicated in HIV-1 PIC nuclear import.
source: Both of these proteins have been implicated in HIV-1 PIC nuclear import (Matreyek and Engelman, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: CPSF6 exhibits an almost exclusively nuclear localization with very weak cytoplasmic staining in TZM-bl cells.
source: Immunostaining of CPSF6 revealed an almost exclusively nuclear localization of this protein with very weak cytoplasmic staining in TZM-bl cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), consistent with previously published reports (De Iaco et al., 2013; Fricke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and citations.

claim: A clear CPSF6 signal co-localizing with the RTC/PIC was detected in 22% of all cases in TZM-bl cells.
source: Nevertheless, a clear CPSF6 signal co-localizing with the RTC/PIC was detected in 22% of all cases in TZM-bl cells (Figure 6A; 92 RTC/PIC analyzed).

claim: TNPO3 knock-down leads to cytoplasmic accumulation of CPSF6.
source: This protein functions as a nuclear import factor for CPSF6, andTNPO3 knock-down has been shown to lead to cytoplasmic accumulation of CPSF6 (De Iaco et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: An increased cytoplasmic CPSF6 signal was detected in the TNPO3 knock-down cell line.
source: Accordingly, an increased cytoplasmic CPSF6 signal was detected in the TNPO3 knock-down cell line but not in a control cell line expressing a scrambled shRNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: 87% of all RTC/PIC were positive for CPSF6 upon infection of the TNPO3 knock-down cell line.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we observed that 87% of all RTC/PIC were positive for CPSF6 upon infection of the TNPO3 knock-down cell line (Figure 6B; 87 RTC/PIC analyzed).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Treatment of TNPO3 knock-down cells with 2 µM PF74 during infection strongly reduced the level of CPSF6 association with RTC/PIC to 18%.
source: Treatment of TNPO3 knock-down cells with 2 µM PF74 during infection strongly reduced the level of CPSF6 association with RTC/PIC to 18% (Figure 6C; 74 RTC/PIC analyzed).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The results provide direct evidence for the association of cytoplasmic CPSF6 with the incoming viral capsid.
source: These results provide direct evidence for the association of cytoplasmic CPSF6 with the incoming viral capsid and for competitive inhibition of this interaction by the small molecule inhibitor PF74.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The results provide direct evidence for competitive inhibition of CPSF6-capsid interaction by the small molecule inhibitor PF74.
source: These results provide direct evidence for the association of cytoplasmic CPSF6 with the incoming viral capsid and for competitive inhibition of this interaction by the small molecule inhibitor PF74.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: IN.eGFP/EdU-positive RTC/PIC could be detected in HIV-1 infected MDM.

claim: RTC/PIC were detected at a much lower frequency in MDM compared to TZM-bl cells.
source: IN.eGFP/EdU-positive RTC/PIC could be detected in HIV-1 infected MDM (Figure 7), albeit at a much lower frequency compared to TZM-bl cells.

claim: HIV-1 uptake into macrophages is more specific, but much less efficient than in HeLa-derived cells.

claim: The average number of RTC/PIC detected in macrophages observed at 24 hr or 48 hr after infection was 10- to 50-fold lower compared to HeLa-derived cells infected for 4 hr.

claim: The number of RTC/PIC in macrophages showed significant donor dependent variation.
source: Accordingly, the average number of RTC/PIC detected in macrophages observed at 24 hr or 48 hr after infection was 10- to 50-fold lower compared to HeLa-derived cells infected for 4 hr and showed significant donor dependent variation (Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—source data 1.

claim: A total of 135 RTC/PIC were observed in the cytoplasm of 567 MDM from eight different donors in five independent experiments.
source: Analyzing a total of 567 MDM from eight different donors in five independent experiments, we observed a total of 135 RTC/PIC in the cytoplasm of these cells.

claim: HIV-1 CA was found to be associated with only 44% of cytoplasmic RTC/PIC in MDM.
source: HIV-1 CA was found to be associated with only 44% of these RTC/PIC (Table 1), while >97% of cytoplasmic RTC/PIC were CA-positive in the case of TZM-bl cells.

claim: The decrease in CA-positive RTC/PIC over time indicates time-dependent loss of CA from cytoplasmic RTC/PIC in MDM.
source: The proportion of CA-positive RTC/PIC in MDM decreased over time with ∼50% CA-positive at 24 hr and ∼30% CA-positive at 48 hr (Table 1), indicating time-dependent loss of CA from cytoplasmic RTC/PIC.

claim: MDM lack nuclear DNA synthesis and therefore exhibited almost no nuclear EdU signal.

claim: 70 nuclear PIC were detected in the total of 567 MDM that were analyzed in this study.

source: Surprisingly, almost all nuclear PIC (68 of 70) exhibited a clearly detectable CA signal (Figure 7B,C; Table 1), suggesting that the intact capsid or a capsid-derived structure remains associated with the replication complex during and after nuclear import.

claim: The intact capsid or a capsid-derived structure remains associated with the replication complex during and after nuclear import in MDM.

claim: EdU is incorporated in the position of thymidine in the viral cDNA.

claim: A maximum of 5588 EdU molecules can be expected for the entire double-stranded cDNA of HIV-1 (NL4-3).

claim: Nascent cDNA for vector genomes of 5.4 kb and 3.7 kb could be identified.

claim: Detection of short reverse transcription products, as suggested for abortive infection of resting primary T-cells, may be possible with this method.
